question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Ann Arbor?
body:
## Direct Answer
You find a fractional CRO in Ann Arbor through three main channels: specialized fractional-executive networks (Chief Outsiders, Fractional Officer, Bolster), the University of Michigan and Ann Arbor SPARK entrepreneurial ecosystem, and local RevOps and go-to-market advisors who already operate in the region's SaaS, medtech, and mobility corridors. Start by defining the revenue problem you're solving, then match it to an operator who has run that exact motion — not just a résumé with "CRO" in the title.

Ann Arbor is an unusually rich hunting ground for a fractional Chief Revenue Officer because it sits at the intersection of a top research university, a dense venture-backed startup scene anchored by Ann Arbor SPARK, and mature enterprises in mobility, life sciences, and enterprise software. That means the pool of experienced revenue leaders who will work part-time — one to three days a week, for a fraction of a full-time comp package — is deeper here than in most metros of comparable size. The trick is knowing where those operators cluster, how to vet them, and how to structure the engagement so you get a builder, not a figurehead.

## What exactly is a fractional CRO and when does an Ann Arbor company need one?
A fractional CRO is a senior revenue executive who takes ownership of your entire go-to-market engine — sales, marketing alignment, customer success, pricing, and revenue operations — but on a part-time or contract basis rather than as a full-time hire. Unlike a consultant who delivers a slide deck and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a quota-adjacent mandate: they own the number, build the team, install the process, and stay accountable for pipeline and net revenue outcomes over a defined engagement, typically three to twelve months.

The Ann Arbor companies that get the most value from this model share a profile. They are usually post–product-market-fit but pre–Series B: annual recurring revenue somewhere between roughly one and fifteen million dollars, a founder or first sales hire who has stopped scaling, and a board or investor pushing for repeatable, forecastable growth. A founder-led SaaS company spun out of U-M research, a medtech firm graduating from grant funding to commercial sales, or a mobility supplier trying to build an enterprise sales motion are all textbook cases. When the revenue problem is *systemic* — bad forecasting, no defined sales stages, marketing and sales pointing fingers — a fractional CRO fixes the machine. When the problem is simply "we need more reps dialing," you want a sales manager, not a CRO. Diagnosing that difference correctly is the single most important step, and it's worth reading our primer on [when to hire a fractional revenue leader](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-hire-signals) before you start any outreach.

## Where do I actually find candidates in and around Ann Arbor?
There are five practical channels, and the best searches use several in parallel rather than betting on one. The first is the **fractional-executive networks** that vet and place these operators nationally but staff regionally: Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Fractional Officer, Continuum, and Go Fractional all maintain rosters of revenue leaders, many of whom live in or will travel to the Detroit–Ann Arbor corridor. These networks pre-screen for the operating experience most founders can't assess on their own, which shortens your vetting cycle considerably.

The second channel is the **Ann Arbor and Southeast Michigan startup ecosystem itself.** Ann Arbor SPARK — the region's economic development and entrepreneurial support organization — runs mentor-in-residence programs, an entrepreneur boot camp, and an investor network, and its staff can often make warm introductions to revenue operators who have exited or advise locally. The University of Michigan's Zell Lurie Institute at the Ross School of Business and the Center for Entrepreneurship in the College of Engineering both maintain alumni and mentor networks heavy with commercial leadership talent. The third channel is **local RevOps and go-to-market advisory firms and independents** who already work with Michigan-based companies; many market themselves as fractional revenue leaders even if they don't use that exact title. The fourth is **your investor and board network** — Michigan-based funds like Renaissance Venture Capital, Grand Ventures, and Detroit-area firms have portfolio-wide talent networks and frequently share fractional operators across companies. The fifth is **LinkedIn and warm referral**, which remains, unglamorously, the highest-hit-rate channel of all when you search by location plus "fractional CRO," "fractional VP Sales," or "revenue advisor."

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Define the revenue problem] --> B{Systemic or tactical}
  B -->|Systemic| C[Fractional CRO search]
  B -->|Tactical| D[Sales manager or rep]
  C --> E[Fractional networks]
  C --> F[Ann Arbor SPARK and UM]
  C --> G[Investor and board referrals]
  C --> H[LinkedIn regional search]
  E --> I[Shortlist three to five]
  F --> I
  G --> I
  H --> I
  I --> J[Structured vetting]
  J --> K[Scoped engagement]
```

Run at least three of these channels at once. A national network gives you breadth and pre-screening; the local ecosystem gives you operators who understand Michigan's talent market, sales cycles, and the specific rhythms of selling into automotive, health systems, and university procurement. The overlap between those two lists is your strongest shortlist.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I get a builder, not a figurehead?
Vetting a fractional revenue leader is different from vetting a full-time hire because you have less time and the engagement is inherently lower-commitment on both sides. Concentrate your diligence on three things: **pattern match, evidence, and references.** Pattern match means the candidate has personally run the specific motion you need — if you sell six-figure enterprise deals with nine-month cycles, an operator whose whole career was product-led self-serve growth is a mismatch no matter how impressive the logo history. Ask them to walk you through a deal or a quarter, not a philosophy. The good ones get concrete fast: they talk about pipeline coverage ratios, stage conversion, ramp time, and the exact levers they pulled.

Evidence means asking for artifacts and outcomes. A real operator can describe the forecasting cadence they installed, the comp plan they redesigned, the pipeline they built from what starting point to what ending point, and how long it took. Be alert for the figurehead pattern — someone who name-drops strategy but goes vague on execution mechanics. References are the final gate: talk to at least two founders or CEOs the candidate has actually served in a fractional capacity, and ask the disqualifying question directly — *would you hire them again, and what did they get wrong?* Structure the whole process against a defined scorecard so you're comparing candidates on the same axes rather than on charisma. Our guide to [structuring a fractional executive engagement](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-engagement-structure) breaks down the scorecard and the contract terms worth negotiating up front.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate intro] --> B[Pattern match check]
  B --> C[Evidence and artifacts]
  C --> D[Two founder references]
  D --> E{Would you rehire them}
  E -->|Yes| F[Scope thirty day plan]
  E -->|No| G[Pass]
  F --> H[Define success metrics]
  H --> I[Signed engagement]
```

One more filter that matters specifically in a market like Ann Arbor: ask whether they will actually be *in the room.* Some of the best fractional operators are stretched across five clients. For a company that needs hands-on team-building, a leader who can spend one full day a week on-site — or at least in the same time zone and available for live pipeline reviews — beats a bigger name who only shows up on a monthly Zoom.

## What should a fractional CRO engagement cost and how is it structured?
Pricing for fractional revenue leadership varies with scope, seniority, and time commitment, and you should be skeptical of any quote that arrives before scope is defined. The honest answer is that engagements are typically structured one of three ways: a **monthly retainer** for a fixed number of days per month, a **project or milestone fee** for a defined build (say, "install a forecasting system and hire two AEs in ninety days"), or a **retainer plus performance component** tied to pipeline or revenue milestones. What you should insist on is not a specific dollar figure — which depends entirely on your stage and needs — but *clarity*: how many days, which outcomes, what cadence, and a clean exit or conversion clause.

The structural decisions matter more than the headline rate. Define a thirty-day plan and a ninety-day plan before signing, with explicit success metrics — pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, ramp milestones, a hired-and-onboarded rep count. Agree on how the fractional CRO's authority works with your existing team so reps know who they report to. And build in a conversion path: many of the best fractional engagements are auditions for a full-time hire, or a bridge until you can afford one, so it's worth agreeing early on what a transition to permanent — or a clean wind-down — looks like. Founders who skip this step often end up paying senior-operator rates for advice they can't operationalize, which is the most common way these engagements disappoint. We cover the tradeoffs in depth in our breakdown of [fractional versus full-time revenue leadership economics](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-vs-fulltime-cro).

## Does the fractional CRO need to be physically in Ann Arbor?
Not necessarily — and being rigid about geography can cost you the best candidate. The rise of remote and hybrid work has widened the fractional talent pool dramatically, and many companies successfully run a fractional CRO who lives in Chicago, Boston, or Austin and travels in for key weeks. What matters far more than a local zip code is *time-zone alignment, market familiarity, and cadence of presence.* An operator in the Eastern or Central time zone who understands how to sell into automotive OEMs, health systems, or research institutions will serve an Ann Arbor company better than a local generalist who has never run your motion.

That said, physical proximity has real, underrated advantages for early-stage team-building. If your fractional CRO needs to sit next to a first sales hire, run live pipeline reviews, coach on real calls, and read the room during a founder-sales handoff, someone who can be on-site in Ann Arbor one day a week creates compounding value that a fully remote arrangement can't match. The practical resolution is to weigh the *specific work* the role demands: a systems-and-strategy build tolerates remote well; a hands-on player-coach hiring and ramping a team benefits from local presence. Decide which kind of engagement you actually need before you let geography narrow — or over-narrow — your list. And regardless of where they sit, insist on a fixed, predictable presence cadence written into the engagement, because "available as needed" is where fractional relationships quietly decay.

## Related questions
### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns the revenue number and builds the team and systems under a leadership mandate; a consultant advises and delivers recommendations but carries no ongoing accountability for pipeline or hires. Choose the CRO when you need someone accountable for outcomes.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO typically work?
Most engagements run one to three days per week, scaled to your stage and budget. Early team-building often needs the higher end; a systems-and-forecasting fix can succeed on one focused day plus async availability for live reviews.

### Can a fractional CRO help me hire a full-time CRO later?
Yes — one of the strongest uses of a fractional engagement is building the revenue machine and defining the role so precisely that you can hire the right permanent leader, or convert the fractional operator into the full-time seat once you can fund it.

### Is Ann Arbor big enough to find qualified fractional revenue talent?
Yes. Between the University of Michigan alumni network, Ann Arbor SPARK's ecosystem, the broader Detroit metro talent pool, and national fractional networks that staff the region, the supply of qualified revenue operators is deeper than the city's size suggests.

### Should a seed-stage startup hire a fractional CRO?
Usually not a full CRO — at seed stage a fractional VP of Sales or a revenue advisor is a better fit. A CRO becomes valuable once you have early traction and a systemic go-to-market problem to solve, not just a need for more selling activity.

## FAQ
**How quickly can I get a fractional CRO started?**
Faster than a full-time hire — often within two to four weeks. Fractional networks pre-screen candidates, and because the commitment is lower-risk for both sides, the decision cycle compresses. The gating factor is usually your own clarity on scope, not candidate availability.

**What size company is a fractional CRO right for?**
Typically companies with roughly one to fifteen million in ARR that are post–product-market-fit but not yet able or ready to fund a full-time CRO. Below that, a fractional VP of Sales usually fits better; well above it, you likely need a permanent revenue leader.

**Do fractional CROs work with non-software companies?**
Yes. Ann Arbor's medtech, mobility, advanced manufacturing, and professional-services firms all use fractional revenue leaders. Match the operator to your specific sales motion — enterprise, channel, or transactional — rather than assuming the role is SaaS-only.

**How is a fractional CRO different from an interim CRO?**
An interim CRO is a full-time placeholder filling a vacant seat until a permanent hire is made, usually working five days a week. A fractional CRO is a permanent part-time arrangement, working a defined slice of the week on an ongoing basis.

**What's the biggest mistake companies make when hiring one?**
Hiring for a résumé instead of a motion match, and failing to define success metrics up front. A leader with an impressive logo history but no experience running your specific sales cycle will underperform a lesser-known operator who has run exactly your motion.

**How do I know if the engagement is working?**
Track leading indicators from day one: pipeline coverage ratio, forecast accuracy, sales-stage conversion, ramp time for new hires, and whether the team is adopting the process the CRO installed. Meaningful movement should appear within the first sixty to ninety days.

**Can I find a fractional CRO through Ann Arbor SPARK directly?**
SPARK doesn't place executives like a staffing firm, but its mentor networks, entrepreneur programs, and investor connections frequently produce warm introductions to revenue operators. Treat it as a referral channel, not a marketplace.

**Should the fractional CRO or I own the ramp of new sales hires?**
The fractional CRO should own hiring, onboarding, and ramping the revenue team — that's central to the mandate. If they defer all people decisions back to you, you've hired an advisor, not a revenue leader.
